title: Festival of Lights
intro: Six verses from the Bhagavad Gita on light and the inner light, from Dhanteras to Bhai Dooj.

posts.caption: For many, the five days of Diwali, the festival of lights, begin around now with Dhanteras, honouring Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, and Dhanvantari, physician of the gods. Through Bhai Dooj, six verses from the Gita on light. In chapter 15, Krishna names himself as the source of the light in sun, moon and fire.

For many, Naraka Chaturdashi falls this weekend, recalling Krishna's victory over the demon Narakasura; in much of South India this is Deepavali itself, begun with an oil bath before dawn. In this verse Krishna describes a quieter victory over darkness: the lamp of wisdom, lit within.

Happy Diwali. For many, tonight is Lakshmi Puja, when homes glow with rows of lamps (deepavali means "row of lights") and many remember Rama's return to Ayodhya. Here the Gita calls the supreme reality the light of all lights, seated in every heart. Many editions number this verse 13:17.

Diwali's lamps are often read as the victory of knowledge over ignorance, and the Gita uses the same image. When ignorance is cleared away by knowledge of the self, Krishna says, that knowledge shines like the sun. Jnana, knowledge or wisdom, is one of the Gita's great paths, alongside karma (action) and bhakti (devotion).

For many, Govardhan Puja falls around now, recalling how Krishna lifted Govardhan Hill to shelter the people of Vraja from Indra's storms. Here fire, the flame of every diya, becomes an image of inner change: wisdom burns up karma as fire burns fuel. Shankara adds that karma already bearing fruit (prarabdha) runs its course.

Bhai Dooj, falling around now for many, closes the Diwali days, as sisters pray for their brothers' long life and brothers promise their care. These days of light end with a light beyond every lamp: Krishna's supreme abode, which needs no sun, moon or fire. Thank you for celebrating with us.
